title: Numerator
summary: The numerator is the top number of a fraction. It counts how many equal parts you have — in 3/4, the numerator 3 says you have three of the four parts. Explore how the numerator changes the amount the fraction names.

compareCandidate.label: Numerator vs. denominator
compareCandidate.description: The numerator counts the parts you HAVE (top). The denominator counts the equal parts in the WHOLE (bottom). One says 'how many parts', the other says 'parts of what size'.

parts: The top number of a fraction
Raising the numerator enlarges the amount
plainLanguageExplanation: In a fraction, the top number is the numerator. It counts how many equal parts you have or are talking about. In 3/4, the numerator 3 means 'three parts out of the four that make the whole'. The bigger the numerator, the more of the whole you have — 5/4 has more than 3/4 (it is even more than one whole). You read the numerator first: 3/4 is 'three fourths'. Without a denominator, the numerator is just a plain counting number — the denominator tells what the parts are.

whyItMatters: The numerator is where the 'how much' of a fraction lives. Adding, comparing, and understanding fractions all start by reading and using the numerator correctly — it is the part that tells you the size of the share you get.
tagline: The top number that counts parts
didYouKnow: The word 'numerator' comes from the Latin 'numerare', meaning 'to count' — the numerator is literally the number that counts parts.
compareReason: The two halves of a fraction answer different questions — comparing the top counter with the bottom sizer is the fastest way to make both stick.
